title: The martyrs' festival compels speech and displays victory over death
english: Bless, Master. I wanted to remain silent and not publish a tongue speaking rustically, for silence is a great thing whenever the word is cheap, and stillness is admirable when lack of learning is present; and the highest philosopher is one who hides ignorance through silence. This is what I too chose to do, knowing the weakness of my own tongue. But the sight of what I see drags me toward speaking. Since, then, the festival is splendid and the theater is packed, and our assembly is boiling in faith, I will turn to the beginning of my speech with confidence—especially since the Father prays, the Church strives alongside, and the holy martyrs strengthen my weakness for this task.

For these martyrs persuaded old men to complete a long journey with much sweat, and they compelled them to steady their faltering steps by the staff of the word. They urged the female sex to travel together with young men, and they led the infant age crawling here. The martyrs leap against death, laugh at swords, plunder the tyrant's rage, seize death as the agent of immortality, make victory their own in their very fall, and leap through their bodies toward heaven. They scatter their limbs in order to bind their souls; they break the bars of life in order to open the keys of heaven.

Let the one who disbelieves that death has been destroyed, that Hades has been trampled, that its bonds have been torn apart, that the tyrant has been bound—let that one look at the martyrs tumbling against death and acclaiming the victory of Christ. O the wonder! From the time Christ plundered Hades, human beings have triumphed over death. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O Hades, is your victory? (Hosea 13:14 / 1 Corinthians 15:55). Hades has been plundered, and the devil too; he has been stripped of his ancient armor, and he has been cast out from his own dominion.

This section is the opening; the sermon continues in sections 2-3.
orientation: The preacher opens the sermon by explaining why he speaks despite his unpolished tongue, then describes how the holy martyrs draw all ages to the festival and leap against death.

title: The devil caught on his own hook, and heaven opened
english: Just as Goliath had his head cut off with his own sword (1 Samuel 17:51), so too the devil, who gave birth to death, is routed through death. He finds that the easy method of his own deceit is a strong instrument of his own destruction. Impaled on the Godhead as on a hook, having swallowed the familiar bait and seized God instead of a man, the one who thought he was catching is plainly caught.

This is why martyrs leap upon the dragon's head and look down on every kind of torture. For from the time the second Adam brought the first Adam up from the depths of Hades (1 Corinthians 15:45–47), as He brought Jonah up from the sea monster (Jonah 1:17–2:10), and to the shame of the deceiver made the deceived a citizen of heaven, from that time the gates of Hades have been shut and the gates of heaven opened, granting unhindered entrance to those who go up in faith.

Long ago Jacob saw a ladder set up and reaching to heaven, and the angels of God going up and coming down (Genesis 28:12). But now the Lover of mankind, who became man for the sake of man, has kicked the enemy of mankind with the foot of the Godhead, has carried man in the hand of His kindness, and has made it possible to walk the untrodden heights of the sky on human feet.

Then the angels went up and came down; but now the Angel of Great Counsel (Isaiah 9:6) does not go up and come down. For from where, and to where, would He move, who is present everywhere, who fills all things, and who holds the ends of the world in His hand (Psalm 95:4)? For He came down once and went up once, not by any shift of His nature, but by the condescension of His kindness and love for mankind: the Word seated with the Father, the Word dwelling in the womb, the Word found everywhere, and never separated from the God of all.

added_allusions.reason: Goliath beheaded with his own sword (τῷ οἰκείῳ ξίφει τὴν κεφαλὴν ἀπετμήθη)
ὁ δεύτερος τὸν πρῶτον Ἀδάμ: Paul's first and last Adam
Ἰωνᾶν ἐκ τοῦ κήτους; Greek/Hebrew Jonah 2:1-11
κλίμακα ἐστηριγμένην ἕως τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ... ἀγγέλους τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀναβαίνοντας καὶ καταβαίνοντας
ὁ τῆς μεγάλης βουλῆς Ἄγγελος (Isaiah 9:5 LXX)
ἐν τῇ χειρὶ συνέχων τὰ πέρατα (Psalm 94:4 LXX, English 95:4)

translator_notes: Goliath beheaded with his own sword: 1 Samuel 17:51 (LXX 1 Kingdoms 17:51).
'Second Adam ... first Adam' is cited to 1 Corinthians 15:45-47, where Paul speaks of the first and last Adam, the first and second man.
Jonah raised from the sea monster: Greek and Hebrew Jonah 2:1-11 is English Jonah 1:17-2:10; cited in English numbering.
The verb ἀνήγαγεν governs both Adam and Jonah, so the one who brought Adam up is also the one who brought Jonah up ('as He brought Jonah up').
Jacob's ladder with the angels going up and coming down: Genesis 28:12.
'Angel of Great Counsel' (ὁ τῆς μεγάλης βουλῆς Ἄγγελος) is Isaiah 9:5 in the Septuagint, Isaiah 9:6 in English Bibles (the 'Wonderful Counselor' verse); cited in English numbering.
'Holds the ends of the world in His hand' echoes Psalm 94:4 in the Septuagint (ἐν τῇ χειρὶ αὐτοῦ τὰ πέρατα τῆς γῆς), which is Psalm 95:4 in English Bibles; cited in English numbering.

σκιρτῶσιν τὴν τοῦ δράκοντος κεφαλήν uses an intransitive verb with a bare accusative; the page image confirms the printed reading, rendered 'leap upon the dragon's head'. A possible echo of Psalm 91:13 (LXX 90:13, trampling the dragon) or Genesis 3:15 is left uncited as uncertain.

Allusions left uncited as uncertain: 'gates of Hades' (Matthew 16:18, though the sermon uses the phrase in a different sense), 'citizen of heaven' (Philippians 3:20), 'fills all things' (Ephesians 4:10; Jeremiah 23:24), and 'came down once and went up once' (John 3:13; Ephesians 4:9-10).
The wordplay ἄνθρωπος / φιλάνθρωπος / ἀπάνθρωπος is rendered 'man ... Lover of mankind ... enemy of mankind'; ἀπάνθρωπος is literally 'the inhuman one', meaning the devil.

χριστότης ('kindness, goodness', with a play on Christ's name) is rendered 'kindness' both times; φιλανθρώπου χριστότητος is rendered 'His kindness and love for mankind' to keep φιλάνθρωπος visible. The play on Christ's name cannot be kept in English.
αἰθήρ ('upper air') is rendered 'heights of the sky'. μετάβασις φύσεως ('a passing over, a change of nature') is set against συγκατάβασις ('condescension'); rendered 'not by any shift of His nature'.

The print's editorial brackets [κόσμου] and [τοῦ] ... [Θεοῦ] are translated as part of the text ('of the world', 'the God of all') without brackets in the reading column. Without the bracketed supplements the last clause would read 'never separated from all things' (τῶν ὅλων).
Capitalised pronouns (He, His) mark Christ, to keep Him distinct from the devil in this passage.
orientation: The devil, who brought death into being, is undone by death: swallowing the bait of Christ's humanity, he is caught on the hook of His Godhead. Christ brings Adam up from Hades, shuts its gates, opens heaven, and, unlike the angels on Jacob's ladder, comes down and goes up without ever leaving any place, for He fills all things.

title: The devil's short laughter and endless grief
english: Once the devil laughed a broad laugh at human nature, and made merry over our misfortunes as though they were feasts. But his laughter lasted three days, while his lament is everlasting. The broad laughter prepared for him a broader lament: tears that never stop, weeping that finds no comfort, an arrow in the heart.

The Commander forged this arrow by fire against the enemy in the furnace of the Virgin, of such a kind as He willed and in the way He willed. He hardened its edge by the working of the unconquerable Godhead, tempered it in the water of the spotless baptism, sharpened it on the sufferings that knew no passion, and polished it through the mystical resurrection. Then by Himself, with His whole force, He put the accursed one to death.

What words, then, could describe either our joy or his calamity? For he who was once an archangel is now a devil. He who once lived in the heavens is now seen crawling on the earth like a snake (Genesis 3:14). He who once exulted with the cherubim is now shut up in the pen of the swine, in anguish. We shall rout him by setting our minds on the opposite of what he chose, through the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and might for ever and ever. Amen.

added_allusions.reason: ὡς ὄφις ἐπὶ γῆς ... συρόμενος: the curse on the serpent

translator_notes: 'Crawling on the earth like a snake' alludes to the curse on the serpent, Genesis 3:14.
'His laughter lasted three days' refers to the three days of Christ's death and burial; no single verse is cited.
'Furnace of the Virgin' (ἐν τῇ παρθενικῇ καμίνῳ) means the womb of the Virgin, where the Commander (πολέμαρχος, 'war-leader') forged the arrow, that is, the Incarnation.
The smith's sequence is kept: στομόω 'harden the edge', βάπτω 'dip' (the quench-tempering of steel, with a play on βάπτισμα 'baptism'), ἀκονάω 'whet', στιλβόω 'polish'.
ἀπαθέσι παθήμασιν is a deliberate paradox ('passionless sufferings'), rendered 'the sufferings that knew no passion'.
πανστρατιᾷ ('with the whole army, in full force') is joined with δι' ἑαυτοῦ ('by himself'): Christ alone acts as a whole army; rendered 'by Himself, with His whole force'.
ἀλάστωρ ('avenging spirit; accursed wretch' in LSJ; used of the devil in Lampe) is rendered 'the accursed one'.
τροπωσόμεθα is rendered 'rout' to match τροποῦται ('is routed') in the previous section; φιλανθρωπία in the doxology is rendered 'love for mankind', matching 'Lover of mankind' there.

ἐπευφραίνεται is present tense in a past narrative and is rendered in the past for clarity. θρῆνον ... πλατύτερον pairs a masculine noun with a neuter-looking comparative, as printed; the sense is clear ('a broader lament').

φυλακή τῶν χοίρων is rendered 'the pen of the swine'; φυλακή may also mean 'prison' (compare Revelation 20:7). The allusion to the swine of Matthew 8:30-32 and Mark 5:11-13 is possible, not certain, and is left uncited.

Other allusions left uncited as uncertain: the fall from heaven (Luke 10:18; Isaiah 14:12) and exulting with the cherubim (Ezekiel 28:14). The closing doxology is a liturgical formula and is not cited.
Capitalised pronouns (He, His, Himself) mark Christ; lowercase pronouns mark the devil.
orientation: The devil's laughter at human misfortune lasted three days, but his grief is endless. Christ forged in the Virgin's womb the arrow that killed him, and the fallen archangel now crawls like a snake. The sermon ends by calling the hearers to rout him by choosing the opposite of what he chose, and closes with a doxology.
